questions.question: The Jhakrana goat breed is native to which Indian state?
questions.explanation: Jhakrana goats originate from the Jhakrana village in Alwar, Rajasthan. They are primarily milch goats, producing good-quality milk with high-fat content.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which of the following breeds is known as the "Dairy Goat of India" due to its high milk production?
questions.explanation: Jamunapari goats are excellent milk producers, often yielding 3-4 liters of milk per day, making them ideal for dairy farming.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which goat breed is mainly found in Punjab and is similar to the Jamunapari breed?
questions.explanation: Beetle goats, found in Punjab, resemble Jamunapari and are famous for both milk and meat production. They have a roman nose and drooping ears.[cite: 20]

questions.question: The Sirohi goat breed is well adapted to which type of climate?
questions.explanation: Sirohi goats, native to Rajasthan, are highly drought-resistant and thrive in hot and arid climates with limited water availability.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which breed is known for its strong adaptability to desert conditions?
questions.explanation: Marwari goats, found in the desert regions of Rajasthan, are highly adaptable to harsh climatic conditions and are primarily raised for meat production.[cite: 20]

questions.question: The Kutchi goat breed is mainly found in which Indian state?
questions.explanation: The Kutchi goat is native to Gujarat, especially in the Kutch region. It is medium-sized, hardy, and suitable for both milk and meat production.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which goat breed from Kerala is known for its high twinning ability and adaptability?
questions.explanation: Malabari goats, originating from Kerala, are highly prolific and known for their high twinning and triplet birth rates, making them excellent for meat and milk production.[cite: 20]

questions.question: The Black Bengal goat is famous for which characteristic?
questions.explanation: Black Bengal goats, primarily found in West Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha, are small-sized but known for their excellent meat quality and high fertility rates.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which goat breed is widely found in Maharashtra and is known for both meat and milk production?
questions.explanation: Osmanabadi goats, native to Maharashtra, are dual-purpose breeds known for their good milk yield and superior meat quality[cite: 20]

questions.question: Ganjam goats are predominantly found in which Indian state?
questions.explanation: Ganjam goats, native to Odisha, are medium-sized, hardy, and primarily reared for meat production.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which goat breed from Maharashtra is mainly reared for meat production and is well adapted to dry conditions?
questions.explanation: Sangamneri goats, found in Maharashtra, are medium-sized, hardy, and mainly reared for meat production, making them ideal for dry and semi-arid regions.[cite: 20]

questions.question: At what age can a doe be first mated for optimal reproductive performance?
questions.explanation: A doe can be mated at 10 to 15 months, ensuring that it kids between 15 to 20 months of age, which optimizes reproductive efficiency.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the average gestation period of a goat?
questions.explanation: The average gestation period of goats is 151 days, though it can vary by ± 3 days depending on the breed and environmental conditions.[cite: 20]

questions.question: How many times can some goats be made to kid in an 18-month period?
questions.explanation: Some goats can kid twice in an 18-month period, depending on their breed and reproductive management practices.[cite: 20]

questions.question: At what age do goats reach their maximum reproductive efficiency?
questions.explanation: Goats reach their maximum reproductive efficiency at 5 to 7 years of age, making it their prime breeding period.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Until when can a well-maintained doe be milked?
questions.explanation: A well-maintained doe can continue to be milked until a month before she is expected to kid again, ensuring good udder health and proper lactation.[cite: 20]

questions.question: How many times can a sow farrow in a year under optimal management?
questions.explanation: Pigs are highly prolific, and under proper management, a sow can farrow twice a year, producing 6-12 piglets per farrowing.[cite: 20]

questions.question: At what age can a sow be first bred?
questions.explanation: A sow can be bred as early as 8-9 months of age to ensure early reproduction and high productivity.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the ideal age to castrate male piglets not selected for breeding?
questions.explanation: Male piglets should be castrated at 3-4 weeks to prevent boar odor in the meat, ensuring better quality pork.[cite: 20]

questions.question: How many sows should be maintained per boar for maximum fertility?
questions.explanation: For every 10 sows, one boar should be maintained to ensure maximum fertility and efficient breeding.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the estrus cycle length in sows?
questions.explanation: A sow comes into heat approximately every 21 days, making it easy to plan breeding schedules.[cite: 20]

questions.question: When is the best time to breed a sow for maximum conception?

options.d: Any time during the heat cycle

questions.explanation: The ideal time to breed a sow is 12 to 24 hours after the onset of heat, which ensures maximum fertility and conception rates.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the gestation period of a pig?
questions.explanation: The gestation period of a pig is three months, three weeks, and three days or approximately 115 days, with a range of 111 to 120 days.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What does the term "farrowing" refer to?
questions.explanation: Farrowing is the act of a sow giving birth to a litter of piglets. It can also refer to the litter itself.[cite: 20]

questions.question: How many times should a sow farrow in a year under proper management?
questions.explanation: Under optimal management, a sow should farrow twice a year to maintain productivity and prevent excessive stress on the animal.[cite: 20]

questions.question: After how many farrowings should old pigs be culled?
questions.explanation: Old sows should be culled after 10-12 farrowings as their reproductive efficiency declines with age.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the ideal weaning period for piglets (separation from the mother)?
questions.explanation: Piglets are typically weaned after 2 months (60 days) to ensure proper development and growth before separation from the mother.[cite: 20]

questions.question: At what age should uncastrated males and females be separated to prevent unwanted mating?
questions.explanation: Uncastrated males and females should not be housed together beyond four months to avoid accidental mating and maintain controlled breeding.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the recommended covered area for housing a boar (male pig)?
questions.explanation: A boar pen should have a covered area of 6-7 m² and an open area of 8-12 m² for exercise.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the minimum height of walls required for a boar pen?
questions.explanation: The walls of a boar pen should have a minimum height of 1.5 m to prevent the boar from escaping and to ensure safety.[cite: 20]

questions.question: How many female pigs (sows) can be housed in a single pen under group housing?
questions.explanation: Sows can be housed in group pens with an area of 2 m² per animal, accommodating 10-15 females per pen.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the recommended area for a farrowing pen (for sows giving birth)?
questions.explanation: Farrowing sows (pregnant sows ready to give birth) should be housed in a farrowing pen of 2.5 x 4.0 m = 10.0 m² which includes guard rails, creep area, and feeding/water troughs.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the recommended space requirement per growing or finishing pig?
questions.explanation: Growing and finishing pigs should be housed in pens providing 2.0 m² per pig, including a covered concrete yard for feeding/resting and an open yard for movement.[cite: 20]

questions.question: How much open area should be provided per buffalo in a well-managed housing system?
questions.explanation: Buffaloes need 25-35 sq. feet of covered space and 80-100 sq. feet of open space to ensure adequate movement and comfort.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the minimum recommended covered space for a pregnant cow?
questions.explanation: Pregnant cows require 100-120 sq. feet of covered space and 180-200 sq. feet of open space for comfort and ease during late pregnancy.[cite: 20]

questions.question: How much open area is required per cow for comfortable housing?
questions.explanation: Cows need 20-30 sq. feet of covered space and 80-100 sq. feet of open space to ensure proper movement and comfort.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the recommended floor space for young stock in the covered area?
questions.explanation: Young stock requires 15-20 sq. feet of covered space and 50-60 sq. feet of open space for proper growth and movement.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the minimum floor space required per ram or buck when housed in groups?
questions.explanation: Rams or bucks housed in groups require a minimum of 1.8 m² per animal to ensure proper movement, feeding space, and reduced aggression.[cite: 20]

questions.question: How much individual floor space is required for a single ram or buck?
questions.explanation: When kept individually, a ram or buck requires 3.2 m² of floor space to provide enough room for resting, feeding, and movement.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the minimum space requirement per lamb or kid when housed in groups?
questions.explanation: Lambs or kids housed in groups require at least 0.4 m² per animal to allow proper growth and movement.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the minimum floor space required for a weaner (young sheep/goat) housed in groups?
questions.explanation: Weaners (young sheep or goats separated from their mothers) require 0.8 m² per animal when housed in groups to ensure healthy growth and feeding space.[cite: 20]

questions.question: How much floor space should be provided for an ewe or doe housed in groups?
questions.explanation: Ewes or does housed in groups require 1.0 m² of space per animal for proper movement and comfort.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the recommended floor space for an ewe with a lamb?
questions.explanation: An ewe with a lamb requires at least 1.5 m² of floor space to ensure both the mother and lamb have adequate room for resting and nursing.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the definition of castration?

options.a: The removal of reproductive organs to prevent reproduction
options.b: The separation of young ones from their mother
options.c: The process of assisting a female animal during parturition
options.d: The practice of selective breeding in livestock
options.e: The removal of horns in cattle and goats

questions.explanation: Castration is the process of removing or inactivating the testicles in male animals to prevent reproduction and improve meat quality.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the purpose of castration in farm animals?

options.b: To reduce aggression and improve meat quality
options.c: To enhance milk production in females
options.d: To increase the growth rate of animals

questions.explanation: Castrated males (such as steers, wethers, or barrows) are less aggressive and produce better-quality meat with improved tenderness.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is weaning in livestock management?

options.a: The removal of testicles in male animals
options.b: The process of removing young ones from their mother's milk
options.c: The act of assisting in animal birth
options.e: The selection of animals for breeding

questions.explanation: Weaning is the process of transitioning young animals from their mother's milk to solid food, usually done at a specific age to ensure proper growth and development.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the benefit of early weaning in farm animals?

options.a: Faster weight gain and efficient feed conversion
options.c: Reduced chances of disease transmission from mother to offspring

questions.explanation: Early weaning helps in better weight gain, improved feed efficiency, and reduces stress on the mother, leading to higher milk yield.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is dehorning in livestock management?

options.a: The removal of reproductive organs in male animals
options.b: The process of removing or preventing horn growth in animals
options.c: The process of assisting an animal during birth
options.d: The removal of tails in sheep to prevent infections

questions.explanation: Dehorning is the process of removing horns or preventing their growth in young animals to reduce injuries and make handling easier.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a common method of dehorning?
questions.explanation: Vaccination does not prevent or remove horns. Dehorning is typically done using chemicals, hot iron, or surgical methods.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the best method to prevent horn growth in newborn calves?

options.c: Applying caustic chemicals to horn buds
options.d: Cutting the horns at 1 year of age

questions.explanation: Caustic chemicals (like potassium hydroxide applied to horn buds in newborns) prevent horn growth by killing horn-producing cells.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the term used for removing testicles from male animals to prevent reproduction?
questions.explanation: Castration is the removal of testicles in male animals to prevent breeding, reduce aggression, and improve meat quality.[cite: 20]

questions.question: At what age are calves typically castrated?
questions.explanation: Calves are usually castrated at 8-10 weeks of age to reduce stress and improve meat quality.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the ideal age for weaning a calf?
questions.explanation: Calves are weaned at around 90 days (8-12 weeks) to transition them from milk to solid feed for proper growth.[cite: 20]

questions.question: At what age are lambs typically castrated?
questions.explanation: Lambs are castrated at 2 weeks of age to minimize stress and complications.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the usual weaning age for lambs?
questions.explanation: Lambs are weaned at around 14 weeks, allowing them to develop properly before full independence from their mother's milk.[cite: 20]

questions.question: At what age are kids (young goats) usually castrated?
questions.explanation: Castration of kids is done at 2-4 weeks of age to prevent breeding and aggression in males.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the weaning age of a kid (young goat)?
questions.explanation: Goat kids are weaned at 16 weeks to ensure proper nutritional transition from milk to solid feed.[cite: 20]

questions.question: At what age are piglets commonly castrated?
questions.explanation: Piglets are castrated at 1 week of age to reduce aggression and improve meat quality.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the typical weaning age for piglets?
questions.explanation: Piglets are weaned at around 8 weeks of age to ensure they can consume solid feed efficiently.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which type of milk has the lowest fat content?
questions.explanation: Skim milk has only 0.5% fat, making it the lowest in fat content.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the fat percentage in double-toned milk?
questions.explanation: Double-toned milk contains 1.5% fat and is commonly consumed as a low-fat option.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which of the following has a fat percentage of 3.0%?
questions.explanation: Toned milk, sheep milk, goat milk, and recombined milk all contain around 3.0% fat.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the fat content of standard milk?
questions.explanation: Standard milk contains 4.5% fat and is richer compared to toned and cow milk.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which animal's milk has the highest fat content among the following?
questions.explanation: Buffalo milk has 5.0% fat, making it one of the richest in fat content.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the fat percentage in cow milk?
questions.explanation: Cow milk has a standard fat percentage of 3.5%, making it a balanced dairy choice.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which of the following is the temperature-time combination for Low-Temperature Long-Time (LTLT) pasteurization?
questions.explanation: LTLT (Batch Pasteurization) involves heating milk at 63°C for 30 minutes to eliminate harmful microbes while preserving milk quality.[cite: 20]

questions.question: High-Temperature Short-Time (HTST) pasteurization is also known as?
questions.explanation: HTST (Flash Pasteurization) rapidly heats milk to 72°C for 15 seconds, effectively killing pathogens while maintaining quality.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the temperature and time combination for Ultra-High Temperature (UHT) pasteurization?
questions.explanation: UHT pasteurization sterilizes milk by heating it to 135°C for 2-5 seconds, extending shelf life without refrigeration.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which type of pasteurization is used for making long-shelf-life milk that does not require refrigeration?
questions.explanation: UHT pasteurization extends the shelf life of milk for months without refrigeration.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the purpose of pasteurization?

options.a: To increase the fat content of milk
options.b: To improve the taste of milk

questions.explanation: Pasteurization is a heat treatment process that eliminates harmful bacteria like Salmonella and E. coli, making milk safe for consumption.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which pasteurization method is commonly used in dairy farms for small-scale processing?
questions.explanation: LTLT pasteurization is widely used in small dairy farms and household-level milk processing.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which of the following pasteurization methods best preserves the taste and nutritional quality of milk?
questions.explanation: HTST pasteurization kills bacteria quickly while preserving the taste and nutritional value of milk better than UHT.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the primary pigment responsible for the bright red color of fresh meat?
questions.explanation: Oxymyoglobin is responsible for the bright red color of fresh meat when exposed to oxygen.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What causes meat to turn brown due to oxidation?
questions.explanation: Metmyoglobin forms when myoglobin is oxidized, giving the meat a brownish color.[cite: 20]

questions.question: The pink color of cured meat is due to which pigment?
questions.explanation: Nitro-haemochromogen is formed in cured meat due to the reaction between myoglobin and nitrites, resulting in a pink color.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is "variety meat" also known as?
questions.explanation: Variety meat refers to edible animal organs like liver, kidney, heart, tongue, brain, and thymus.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which type of meat contains the highest amount of vitamin B12 and folic acid?
questions.explanation: Beef and mutton are rich sources of vitamin B12 and folic acid, which are essential for red blood cell formation.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which meat contains 5-10 times more vitamin B1 (Thiamine) than beef and mutton?
questions.explanation: Pork is significantly rich in vitamin B1 (Thiamine), an essential nutrient for energy metabolism.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the correct definition of bacon?

options.a: Meat from the thigh of a pig
options.b: Meat from the sides and back of a pig
options.c: Meat from the ribs of a pig
options.d: Meat from the shoulders of a pig
options.e: Meat from the belly of a pig

questions.explanation: Bacon is a cured meat product made from the sides and back of a pig.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the correct definition of ham?

options.a: Meat from the ribs of a pig
options.b: Meat from the belly of a pig
options.c: Meat from the thigh or buttocks of a pig
options.d: Meat from the back of a pig

questions.explanation: Ham is taken from the hind leg of a pig and is commonly cured or smoked.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is "prime pork"?

options.c: Meat from a castrated male or virgin female pig
options.d: Meat from the head of a pig

questions.explanation: Prime pork comes from young, castrated males or virgin female pigs for better meat quality.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which of the following is considered "white meat"?
questions.explanation: Poultry (chicken and turkey) is classified as white meat due to its lower myoglobin content compared to red meat.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which vitamin is found in the highest amount in animal meat?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 is found abundantly in animal meat and is essential for neurological function and red blood cell formation.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which vitamin is found in the highest amount in poultry meat?
questions.explanation: Poultry meat is rich in niacin (vitamin B3), which is important for metabolism and skin health.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which meat lacks Vitamin A?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A is absent in buffalo meat, goat meat (chevon), and pork, but it is found in beef and mutton.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What type of meat is obtained from cattle?
questions.explanation: Beef is the meat obtained from cattle (cows, bulls, and steers).[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the meat of a goat called?
questions.explanation: Chevon is the term for goat meat, commonly consumed in many parts of the world.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Mutton is the meat of which animal?
questions.explanation: Mutton is the meat of an adult sheep, usually over one year old.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the term for the meat obtained from a young calf?
questions.explanation: Veal is the tender meat obtained from young calves, usually less than six months old.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Pork is the meat of which animal?
questions.explanation: Pork refers to the meat obtained from pigs and is widely consumed worldwide.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What type of meat is obtained from a rabbit?
questions.explanation: Rabbit meat is called "Lapin" and is a lean source of protein.[cite: 20]

questions.question: The meat obtained from a young sheep (less than one year old) is called?
questions.explanation: Lamb is the meat from young sheep under one year of age, which is more tender than mutton.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the meat of a wild boar called?
questions.explanation: Wild boar meat is called "boar meat" and is a game meat that has a stronger flavor than regular pork.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the name of the meat obtained from a buffalo?
questions.explanation: Buffalo meat is called "Buff" and is similar to beef but leaner.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Poultry meat refers to the meat obtained from which of the following?
questions.explanation: Poultry meat includes chicken, turkey, duck, and other domesticated birds.[cite: 20]

questions.question: Which of the following is known as "white meat"?
questions.explanation: Poultry (chicken, turkey, etc.) is considered white meat due to its low myoglobin content.[cite: 20]

questions.question: What is the name of the meat obtained from a duck?
questions.explanation: Duck meat is a type of poultry, but it has a darker and richer flavor than chicken.[cite: 20]
